name: Graston Technique

card.summary: A trademarked instrument-assisted soft-tissue therapy in which stainless-steel tools are used on muscle and connective tissue, used by lifters and athletes for recovery and mobility.
card.note: Bruising is a commonly cited effect of tool-based soft-tissue work.

quick.overview:
The Graston Technique uses a set of six stainless-steel instruments that a trained practitioner draws across skin and soft tissue to find and treat adhesions in muscles, tendons and fascia. It was started by David Graston and is licensed through Graston Technique, LLC.

For looks it is a recovery chain: easing pain and stiffness may let people keep training, and consistent training builds the physique. Trials mostly look at pain, range of motion and function in conditions such as low back pain, plantar heel pain and neck pain.
quick.how: Practitioners warm the area, scrape the tools along the tissue and often follow with stretching or exercise. It is used in sports medicine, chiropractic and physiotherapy, and lifters mention it in training logs. Sessions typically recur over weeks.
quick.risks: The technique is a hands-on treatment in which discomfort during treatment and skin marks afterward are commonly described. Practitioners should be trained and licensed in the method, and individuals with skin or bleeding conditions would seek medical advice first.

lead: The Graston Technique is a trademarked form of instrument-assisted soft-tissue mobilization (IASTM) in which a trained clinician draws a set of six stainless-steel instruments across the skin over muscles, tendons and fascia to find and treat areas of restriction, often described as scar tissue or adhesions.[1][2] It was started by David Graston, covered by a US patent issued in 1993, and is licensed through Graston Technique, LLC, which also runs the training courses for clinicians.[1][3]

For appearance, the route is mostly through training and recovery. Lifters and athletes use instrument-assisted work on tight or sore areas such as hamstrings, hips, shoulders and forearms in the hope of moving more freely and training with less pain, and consistent training is what builds the physique. Forum training logs describe it as a recovery tool alongside active release therapy, and some posters report immediate relief after a session.[4][5][6]

Research on the technique and on IASTM in general consists of randomised trials of low back pain, plantar heel pain, neck pain, cervicogenic headache, Achilles tendinopathy and shin pain, plus systematic reviews of range of motion in throwing athletes and of spinal pain.[7][8][9][10][11][13][15][18][20][21] Trials usually measure pain, flexibility and function rather than appearance. The Wikipedia article on the method states that its evidence base has been questioned and that high-quality trials are lacking, while the company describes the method as evidence-based.[1][3]

chain: Tools used on tight soft tissue
Less pain and stiffness, better mobility
angle.text: Lifters and athletes use instrument-assisted work to manage soreness and mobility so they can continue training. The appearance benefit comes through sustained training.

paras: The Graston Technique is described as a method for assessing and treating disorders of skeletal muscle and related connective tissue. The clinician uses a hand-held instrument, a lubricating emollient on the skin, and a scraping or stroking motion to detect areas that feel rough, gritty or restricted, then works over them with sustained strokes.[1][3] The instruments come as a six-piece set in stainless steel with different curves and bevelled edges designed to fit different body regions, and the company says only its own instruments, used by certified clinicians, qualify as Graston Technique.[3]

IASTM is the broader category: a 2016 systematic review described it as a treatment for myofascial restriction in which specially designed tools provide a mobilising effect to scar tissue and myofascial adhesions, with the Graston Technique as one of several branded systems.[8] Other tool-based approaches exist, and the technique is also discussed alongside manual methods such as active release therapy and ischaemic compression.[23][19]

Wikipedia credits David Graston with starting the method and records United States patent 5,231,977, titled as tools and a method for soft-tissue massage, issued on 3 August 1993.[1] The technique is trademarked, and practitioners need a licence from Graston Technique, LLC to use the name or the patented instrument set.[1]

In a 2011 T Nation thread a physical therapist wrote that the man who developed the method had sold it and then started a new company with different tools and techniques; this is a forum poster's account and the page does not give details.[6] Competing IASTM tool brands now exist and the Graston company warns that some tools sold as IASTM instruments are counterfeit or of lower quality.[3]

Graston Technique, LLC offers self-paced online courses, live virtual cohorts and multi-day in-person workshops, plus continuing-education short courses and webinars, and designates clinicians who complete training as Certified GT Providers.[3]

The company says the technique helps break down scar tissue and adhesions, improve blood flow and reduce inflammation, which it says can speed recovery and restore movement.[3] Wikipedia summarises the method's theory as using the tools to find and resolve adhesions in muscles and tendons.[1]

The wider IASTM literature frames the goal in terms of treating myofascial restriction and improving joint range of motion.[8] A 2018 critically appraised topic on overhead athletes noted that recommended treatment times differ between studies and that there is no consensus on the appropriate pressure, with positive results reported in studies using about five to six minutes per treatment region.[9]

sections.h: Use in training and looksmaxxing communities
paras: The method appears in strength-training forums mostly as an injury and soreness resource. T Nation posters describe having it applied to hamstrings, hips, adductors, iliopsoas and shoulders, and several describe pain relief afterwards, for example one who wrote that hip pain cleared immediately after sessions and another who reported feeling no pain the next day and continued pressing.[4][12][24]

Descriptions of the experience vary. Posters call the tools metal devices, say the treatment hurts while it is performed, and in one case compare it to an intensified version of active release therapy.[5][23] One lifter in 2023 wrote that he wanted to believe in it but could not find information on how effective it was, noting that heavy bruising in the treated area seemed to need data behind it.[22] Another poster asked about it as a counterpart to gua sha, which they were already trying.[2]

In the appearance context the benefit is indirect: a lifter who can train a joint or muscle group with less discomfort can keep up the volume that builds muscle, and the tool-based work is used between sessions alongside stretching and strength exercises.[4][12]

A 2016 systematic review in the Journal of the Canadian Chiropractic Association appraised seven randomised trials of IASTM. Five compared the technique with a control or another treatment for a musculoskeletal condition and found no significant differences between groups, while two measuring joint range of motion found significant short-term gains lasting up to 24 hours. The authors wrote that the research was still developing and that methodological differences might explain the null findings.[8]

A 2018 critically appraised topic on overhead athletes with shoulder range-of-motion deficits reviewed three studies, two of which found significant acute gains compared with self-stretching; the authors graded this as moderate evidence for acutely increasing range of motion in the glenohumeral joint.[9] A 2026 systematic review of IASTM versus passive stretching in throwers included four of 121 identified studies, all reporting improved shoulder range of motion with IASTM, and the authors described the finding as tentative and in need of larger studies, standardised protocols and long-term follow-up.[10]

A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of the Graston Technique for low back and thoracic spinal pain identified four eligible randomised and non-randomised trials. Pooled data showed a reduction in pain scores compared with placebo (mean difference -1.45 on the visual analogue scale, 95% CI -2.24 to -0.66), with no significant difference compared with active treatments and no significant improvement in disability scores; the authors called the results preliminary.[7]

The Wikipedia article states that there are no high-quality clinical trials validating the technique and that its assumptions are questionable, citing a 2009 critique.[1] The company's website describes the method as evidence-based and links to a research library, and presents clinician testimonials.[3]

Plantar heel pain has been the most-studied condition. A 2019 pilot randomised trial of 11 adults with chronic plantar heel pain compared stretching and exercise with the same programme plus Graston-type IASTM over up to eight visits; both groups improved, between-group effect sizes were medium to large, and the authors judged a larger study feasible.[11] A randomised trial in Faisalabad, Pakistan, of 30 patients with chronic plantar fasciitis found that adding the technique to conventional physical therapy for four weeks produced larger pain improvements than conventional therapy alone at weeks two and four, with no significant difference in general foot health.[13] A 2022 trial of 69 patients with chronic plantar heel pain compared shockwave therapy plus stretching, Graston plus stretching and stretching alone; the two active treatments had similar effects on first-step pain after treatment and at eight weeks, and the Graston group had significantly better Foot Function Index scores at six months.[14]

For the spine, a trial of 30 adults with chronic non-specific low back pain at a university hospital in Turkey gave exercise with or without the technique three times weekly for four weeks; pain and disability improved more in the Graston group, while differences in pressure pain threshold, flexibility, proprioception and quality of life were not significant between groups.[15] A 2017 study of 24 adults with non-specific low back pain compared the technique applied to the hamstrings with static stretching and reported larger gains in hamstring extensibility in the Graston group.[16] A 2016 study examined pain and range of motion in chronic low back pain.[17]

In cervicogenic headache, a single-blinded randomised trial of 60 patients aged 35 to 50 added the technique to an exercise programme for four weeks, with three sessions per week; the Graston group showed statistically significant advantages on pain, headache frequency and duration and medication intake, and the authors cautioned that disability and neck-motion differences were probably not clinically meaningful.[18] A pilot trial compared the technique with ischaemic compression in students with neck pain during pandemic distance learning.[19]

Lower-leg conditions have also been tested. A 2023 randomised trial of 46 participants with medial tibial stress syndrome compared the technique with cupping over three weeks; both groups improved, and the authors concluded cupping may produce better results.[20] A 2024 study of 32 patients with Achilles tendinopathy compared two Graston-based programmes, one with eccentric calf exercises and one with a heel lift, and reported improvement in both.[21]

IASTM sits within a family of hands-on and tool-based soft-tissue methods, including gua sha, which one forum poster described the technique as resembling, as well as active release therapy, ischaemic compression, cupping and shockwave therapy, several of which appear in the comparison trials above.[2][23][14][19][20]

Wikipedia lists the technique among chiropractic-associated methods, alongside others such as the Activator method and Gonstead technique, though the Graston tools are used by physical therapists, athletic trainers and other clinicians as well.[1]

Forum users commonly describe discomfort during treatment and visible marking afterwards; one wrote that it hurt but that pain was gone immediately, and another asked whether the heavy bruising it caused had data behind it.[4][22] The Wikipedia article does not list adverse events specific to the technique.[1]

The company states that its instruments should be used by certified clinicians and warns about counterfeit tools.[3] A critically appraised topic on overhead athletes noted that some IASTM tools require certification to use and that treatment intensity is unsettled.[9]

lore.intro: In strength-training forums the technique is discussed as one of several recovery and soft-tissue tools, often by people recounting a physical therapy session.[4][5][12]

claims.claim: Tool-based scraping breaks up adhesions and scar tissue
claims.believers: Practitioners and the company say the tools detect and treat adhesions and scar tissue, and a poster described therapists using metal tools to break up adhesions in his adductors.[3][5]
claims.experts: Systematic reviews describe IASTM as aimed at myofascial restriction; Wikipedia says its assumptions have been questioned, and trials mainly measure pain and range of motion rather than tissue structure.[1][8]

claims.claim: One session can clear pain immediately
claims.believers: Several lifters on T Nation report relief right after sessions on hips, groin or shoulders.[4][12][24]
claims.experts: A 2016 review found short-term range-of-motion gains lasting up to 24 hours in two trials, and a 2017 study reported immediate hamstring-extensibility gains versus stretching in people with low back pain.[8][16]

claims.claim: It improves flexibility more than stretching
claims.believers: Athletes and clinicians use it to restore shoulder and hamstring motion.[9]
claims.experts: A 2018 appraisal and a 2026 review of throwers report greater short-term shoulder motion than stretching, which the authors call tentative.[9][10]

claims.claim: It speeds recovery from heel pain and tendon problems
claims.believers: Clinicians and patients describe using it for plantar fasciitis, Achilles and elbow tendon problems.[3][5]
claims.experts: Trials in plantar heel pain report larger pain or function gains when added to stretching or therapy, but several are small, and one trial of 11 patients was a pilot.[11][13][14]

claims.claim: Painful, bruising treatment is part of how it works
claims.believers: Posters describe treatment that hurts and leaves marks but is followed by relief, and one lifter asked whether such heavy bruising had data behind it.[4][22]
claims.experts: A critically appraised topic noted there is no consensus on appropriate treatment intensity, and the reviews found do not test whether pressure or bruising relates to outcome.[9]

claims.claim: It works like gua sha or active release therapy
claims.believers: Forum posters compare the technique to gua sha and call it active release therapy with metal tools.[2][23]
claims.experts: Comparative trials exist against cupping, ischaemic compression, shockwave and stretching, with varied outcomes.[14][19][20]
